title: On‑Prem Smoke Investigation Notes and Terraform Module Hints
content:
Purpose:
These are working notes for diagnosing post-install and post-upgrade smoke failures in private (VPC / on‑prem) installs. This doc is intentionally informal — daily triage artifacts, quick troubleshooting commands, heuristics we use in the field, and lightweight Terraform module observations that helped root cause common install/runtime patterns.

Audience:
- SREs and field engineers called for on‑prem incidents
- Solutions engineers doing upgrades/installs at customer sites
- Engs writing or reviewing TF modules for private deployments

Quick index (jump to):
1) First 8 minutes triage checklist
2) Classic failure signatures and what they usually mean
3) Terraform module gotchas and quick fixes
4) Post-upgrade safety checks (preflight + smoke)
5) Example investigative commands and paste-ready snippets
6) Rollback gating and safe rollback recipe
7) Open questions / TODOs / notes to self

1) First 8 minutes triage checklist (fast, low/no-customer-impact checks)
- Confirm customer reports: what failed? (HTTP 5xx, long tails, scheduler crash, pods CrashLoopBackOff).
- Access: can you reach the control plane API from your workstation and from a node in the cluster? (curl to health endpoints).
- Rolling indicator: are the runtime GPUs / device drivers visible? (nvidia-smi, lspci)
- K8s / system: kubectl get nodes/pods -n redwood-system -o wide. Look for NotReady/CrashLoopBackOff/ContainerCannotRun.
- Disk & inode pressure: df -h, df -i on critical mounts (/var/lib/kubelet, /var/log, /srv).
- Network reachability: traceroute to S3/backends, iptables-save, recently applied security group / firewall changes.
- Recent terraform/apply? Look at the TF run log, terraform state lock status, and the CI/CD pipeline invocation time.
- If capacity-related: check autoscaler and pod resource requests vs node allocatable.

Note: these are purposely short, quick checks — avoid heavy inspection if customer is on a live incident (start with read-only ops).

2) Classic failure signatures and heuristics
- Symptom: worker pods stuck in Init or CrashLoop with error "failed to allocate shared memory: permission denied"
  - Likely: ephemeral volume mount permissions or incorrect securityContext for ephemeral mounts (init container created directory owned by root:root but runtime runs under uid 1001).
  - Quick fix: check pod YAML for fsGroup and runAsUser. For immediate triage, exec into init pod (if alive) and inspect dir perms; escalate to patching PodSecurityPolicies or change module to set fsGroup explicitly.

- Symptom: runtime logs show "cudaDriverVersion mismatch" or DevicePlugin reports 0 GPUs
  - Likely: kernel-driver/driver mismatch after node reboot or an automatic kernel upgrade happened. Also seen when rocm driver mismatches.
  - Quick check: ssh node -> nvidia-smi (or rocminfo). If empty, check modprobe and dmesg for driver load errors.
  - Fix path: coordinate with infra to roll driver re-install or pin kernel; for urgent mitigation move affected workloads to other nodes if pool available.

- Symptom: long tail latency, tokens stall at 0.5–1s per token after initial warmup
  - Likely: KV cache thrashing or offload path hitting swap/slow NVMe; observed when cache directory mapped to a disk under heavy IO or when config defaulted to CPU backup.
  - Check: disk io (iostat), kernel swap, runtime config for kv_cache_dir and kv_cache_size.

- Symptom: TF apply errored with "module X: resource exists" during upgrade
  - Likely: partial apply in previous run or manual change outside TF (drift).
  - Recommended: run terraform state list and import resources that are present but not in state, then replan. If it's a sensitive resource (LB, IP), coordinate rollback windows.

3) Terraform module gotchas (notes from field)
- Provider pinning: we saw ~3 installs where provider upgrades changed resource lifecycle semantics (aws_lb -> aws_lb/listeners rearranged). Pin provider versions in env (CLI wrapper that injects TF_VERSION and provider version constraints).
- Outputs that change shape: some modules emit maps vs lists depending on provider version. Add a normalization wrapper in calling module: local.tf -> tomap/tolist guards.
- Module idempotency: ensure module adds owner tags and consistent resource naming (avoid random suffix in control-plane security groups). Random suffixes break upgrade path because TF detects aleady existing resources and tries to create duplicates.
- State locking gotcha: S3-backed state can remain locked if CI runner dies. Always have an 'tf force-unlock' runbook in vault with approvals; log the controller run-id and operator who owns it.
- K8s bootstrap race: module applies k8s resources via provider during bootstrap before the cluster provider has API availability for CRDs (custom resources). Add a retry wrapper or 'wait_for_crd' local-exec step.
- Secrets handling: the module previously wrote secrets to plain S3 during bootstrap; ensure TF module uses KMS-encrypted SSM/SecretsManager or Vault integration.

4) Post-upgrade safety checks (preflight + smoke)
- PRE-UPGRADE (checklist):
  - current traffic baseline snapshot (latency p50/p95, token/sec) saved to artifact storage
  - snapshot of TF state (state backup) and export plan to a file with the run-id
  - document critical resource ids (LB IPs, persistent volume IDs, KMS keys)
  - check node pool autoscaler config and minimum capacity to prevent accidental scale-to-zero
  - check driver/OS package versions pinned in image manifest

- ROLLING UPGRADE SMOKE (post-apply quick tests):
  - Health endpoints: /_internal/health for control plane and runtime endpoints all return 200 within expected latency
  - Minimal inference test: send a 32-token prompt to each deployed model variant (hosted in cluster) and assert response completes within target latency and no decode errors
  - KV cache test: hit same session twice and assert second response token rate is >= first (indicates caching saves time), or check cache hit metric.
  - Disk & IO: run a targeted iostat on nodes that received changes; assert %util not spiking above threshold
  - Telemetry sanity: ingestion pipeline to observability ingest logs and metrics for at least 30 min; verify no regression alerts firing

5) Example investigative commands (paste-ready)
- K8s: kubectl -n redwood-system get pods -o wide || true
- Find recent restarts in last hour: kubectl get pods -n redwood-system --sort-by='{.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount}' -o jsonpath='{range .items[*]}{.metadata.name}:{.status.containerStatuses[0].restartCount}\n'
- Pod logs for failing pod: kubectl -n redwood-system logs deploy/runtime-inference -c runtime --since=60m | sed -n '1,200p'
- Node GPU status: ssh node01 'nvidia-smi -L && systemctl status nvidia-docker || true'
- Check docker/containerd OOMs: journalctl -u kubelet -n 200 | grep -i oom || true
- TF plan diff for a resource: terraform plan -out=upgrade.plan && terraform show -json upgrade.plan | jq '.resource_changes[] | select(.address=="module.runtime.aws_instance.runtime")'

Common log snippets to grep for (useful regexes):
- "permission denied" (file/dir mounts) -> grep -i "permission denied" /var/log/containers/*
- "Failed to load driver" or "no devices were found" -> dmesg | egrep -i "nvidia|cuda|rocm|driver"
- "panic: runtime error" or "segmentation fault" -> grep -R "panic:\|segmentation fault" /var/log/pods || true

6) Rollback gating and safe rollback recipe
- Rollback triggers (pick any):
  - latency/p95 increased > 2x for 15+ minutes AND error rate > 1% absolute increase
  - critical pods in CrashLoop for > 10 minutes across N nodes (N depends on cluster size; default N=2)
  - TF apply failed to complete and left partial resources impacting routing (LB gone, DNS changed)

- Safe rollback steps (high level):
  1. Stop automated rollouts (pause any pipeline or CI job).
  2. Mark the release as "rollback in progress" in incident doc and notify stakeholders.
  3. Re-apply previous TF state snapshot (prefer 'terraform apply' against saved plan to restore only changed resources). If the previous plan not available, use state snapshot restore from S3 and force-unlock state.
  4. Restore Kubernetes manifests from last known-good manifest bundle (we keep previous bundle in S3 with deploy tags).
  5. Validate runtime health via the rolling smoke checks above.
  6. If underlying infra changed (IP/LB), coordinate DNS TTL and client fallback windows.
  7. Post-mortem: capture root causes, add a specific TF module test that prevents the same drift.

7) Open questions, TODOs, notes to self
- TODO: add automated 'wait_for_device_plugin' step to control-plane bootstrap to avoid race with driver driverless nodes (pods pending because no GPUs visible).
- TODO: add a small Terraform acceptance test that runs in CI to detect provider API changes that alter resource shape (map vs list) — maybe run against a light-weight sandbox account.
- Question: should we include a 'dry-run destroy' stage during upgrade canary to ensure no unexpected deletions? Needs product discussion.
- Notes to self: standardize a single 'tf-run-metadata' tag injected into all TF runs (git sha + pipeline id + operator) so we can quickly map state events to CI runs.
- Sticky: sometimes customers reconfigure on-prem firewalls while we are performing upgrade. Add a one-pager with minimal ports and CIDR ranges that must remain open during upgrade (control plane CIDR, artifact storage, KMS endpoints).

Appendix: Quick port list (rough)
- 443 outbound to artifacts S3 and telemetry endpoints
- 2379 tcp to etcd (if external)
- 10250 kubelet from control plane
- custom: 3000-3200 (runtime RPC) — ensure allowed intra-VPC

Appendix: recent incident nugget (example)
- Symptom: after upgrade, we saw sporadic 403s from model service to object storage when fetching model weights.
- Root cause: an IAM role ARN changed due to a terraform module applying a new module that recreated an instance profile with different name. TF plan showed 'forces replacement' but operator missed the replace-before-destroy warning.
- Mitigation taken: re-imported the existing instance profile into TF state and applied a patch so the new module referenced the existing resource instead of creating a new one. Added a guard in the module: lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true } for instance_profile resource in environments where customer-managed IAM is expected.

If you use this doc in an incident, please copy into incident-{YYYYMMDD}-onprem-smoke and add the run-id + timeline.

End of notes.
